paragraphs.source_en: AST & Science, which is a US-based company, got its launch license in Papua New Guinea. Why do this? Quite possibly because that country has not signed either the Liability or Registration Conventions. As James Dunstan pointed out in an article on the topic, the value of the satellites in orbit would be larger than Papua New Guinea’s entire governmental budget, raising concerns about their ability to pay for damages even if they did agree they were liable.

paragraphs.source_en: In 1963 the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty prohibited testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere or outer space. That same year the USSR and the United States agreed to a resolution in the UN agreeing not to orbit nuclear weapons in space either. With the arrival of the OST four years later, “weapons of mass destruction” in general were banned from outer space. But, guess what—“weapons of mass destruction” is also not defined. Nuclear weapons are specifically ruled out, and international law in general rules out biological and chemical weapons.

units.source_en: In 1963 the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty prohibited testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere or outer space.
That same year the USSR and the United States agreed to a resolution in the UN agreeing not to orbit nuclear weapons in space either.
With the arrival of the OST four years later, “weapons of mass destruction” in general were banned from outer space.
But, guess what—“weapons of mass destruction” is also not defined.
Nuclear weapons are specifically ruled out, and international law in general rules out biological and chemical weapons.

paragraphs.source_en: However, at least in principle, a country could orbit enough regular old missiles to enact quite a good amount of destruction, and it’d probably be legal as long as none of those missiles had a nuclear tip. Also, you can’t have a Moon fort. No off-world “military bases, installations and fortifications.” No military maneuvers in space either, although you are specifically allowed to put military people in space for peaceful reasons—a sensible policy from a time when most spacefarers were military test pilots.
